job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Nikhil Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a seven-person startup in Bristol that builds sensors for cold-storage warehouses. I studied electrical engineering with a software minor, and my final project was a battery monitor for a student racing team. A normal day is soldering in the morning, writing firmware with an AI assistant in the afternoon, and arguing with my co-founder boss, Dev, about priorities over a very bad coffee.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part of the job, and what's the hardest part?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that I get to build a real thing from start to finish, and that I'm trusted with it. What I hate is the money. I'm on a low salary with a big loan, I share a flat with three people, and I have about two weeks of savings. If the startup missed its next funding round, I'd have a month at most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, and I'd also say the hype was loud. I use AI every day and it helps, but it's like a better spell-checker for code, not a colleague. I'd tell friends that nothing breaks, so don't panic and don't gamble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the thing that scares me in that world isn't AI at all. It's the startup running out of money. Funding is tight, our runway is nine months, and a quiet world means investors stay cautious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building and I'd learn the hardware side more deeply, because boards and sensors are physical and customers pay for them. I'd move 80 a month into savings and start a small side gig doing firmware fixes for a friend's company at weekends. I'd also keep my CV updated every quarter, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit knotted. Excited by the work, worried about money, and I can't quite make those two stop arguing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said runway is nine months. How do you know that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev told us at the Monday meeting, in a flat voice. I did the maths on the back of a napkin afterwards: nine months of pay for seven people, and one new client wouldn't change that much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dev if the money dried up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to take a pay cut for two months if it kept the team together. I wouldn't do it for ever, but I'd rather be in the room than outside it.

say: AI helps every day, but it's a **better spell-checker**, not a colleague.
I'd tell friends not to panic and not to gamble.
think: What scares me is the **startup running out** of money, not AI.
Funding is tight, and our **runway** is about nine months.
do: Learn the **hardware side** deeper, since customers pay for boards and sensors.
Save **80 a month** and do weekend firmware fixes for a friend's company.
Update my CV every quarter, just in case.
feel: **Knotted**: excited by the work and worried about money at once.
S0.quote: I'd offer to take a pay cut for two months if it kept the team together.
fieldNote: His anxiety is about the **startup's cash**, a pressure he carries in every scenario.
Fluent with AI but doesn't think it solves his money problem.
Loyal to his team, with a limit.

steps.text: Take on a weekend firmware job for a friend's company
Learn PCB layout and power design at work
Keep building the sensor firmware and shipping to clients

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's exciting and a bit scary, and I'd tell friends the same. I already see junior roles in software being cut on job boards, so I'd say we should learn the tools and not wait for permission.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm in a better spot than most graduates because I can do hardware and software. Yet writing firmware is exactly the coding the card mentions. If the AI writes ninety percent, then the startup needs one engineer, not three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go deeper into AI tools, so I'm the person who tells them what to build. I'd ask Dev if I can lead the customer integration work, since talking to people is hard to automate. I'd also start a small open-source project to show my skills, and I'd keep my rent flat by staying with my housemates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert, I'd say. Fired up and a bit nervous, like before a race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one engineer instead of three. Who would the one be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like it to be me, but Dev's co-founder Meera has ten years in embedded systems. So I'd need to be the person who connects the AI tools, customers and the hardware.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does that fit with your belief in unions and public support?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a gap, I know. I'd do the personal plan and also say loudly that people who lose junior jobs need support, because my plan doesn't help my flatmate in accounts.

feel: **Fired up** and nervous, like the minutes before a race.

fieldNote: He is adaptable and hopeful but sees the **gap** between his plan and what others get.

Progressive values show up as a call for support.

steps.text: Use AI tools for all firmware drafts and review them carefully
Publish an open-source sensor library to show my skills
Sign and share a petition for retraining support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and nobody is ready, and I'd say it publicly. I'd tell friends that governments need to talk about basic income and retraining this year, not in 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think the coding part of my job goes quickly, and the startup may not survive the shake-up. My hardware skills help for the three years before robots arrive, but not for long. I'm frightened that I'll hit 2028 with a loan and no job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using every AI tool I can find to build products on my own, and try to launch something small before the end of 2027. I'd move to the cheapest room I can find and cut my spending to bare bones. I'd also join a union or a group for tech workers, because I think we'll need to bargain together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mixture of dread and a weird kind of excitement. I'd rather be in the middle of it than watching it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of product could you launch alone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something for cold storage, since I know the customers: a sensor that reports to an AI that books repairs. I'd rather build one tool people use than apply to fifty jobs that no longer exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, because they're far away and would worry. I'd tell my flatmates, though, and we'd agree to cover each other's bills for a month if one of us got stuck.

say: Nobody is ready, and **governments** must plan basic income and retraining this year.
I'd say so publicly and tell friends the same.
think: The **coding part** of my job goes quickly, and the startup may not survive.
My hardware skills help only for the **three years** before robots arrive.
do: Build a small **cold-storage product** with AI tools before the end of 2027.
Move to the **cheapest room** I can find.
Join a **tech workers' group** to bargain together.
feel: **Dread** mixed with a strange excitement, and I'd rather be in the middle of it.
S2.quote: I'd rather build one tool people use than apply to fifty jobs that no longer exist.
fieldNote: He turns the shock into a **launch plan**, which keeps his mood at anxious, not alarmed.
The house-share agreement shows a collective instinct.

steps.text: Build and sell a repair-booking sensor to cold-storage firms
Move to the cheapest room in the city
Join a tech workers' group and attend its meetings
Use AI tools to speed up design and testing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough time to do something about it. I'd say publicly that we should use the time to build up retraining and fair rules, and I'd say the next few elections should be about this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd see it as a window. The first two years I'd get as much real experience as I can while the startup is alive, then I'd choose between starting something or moving into a role that supervises AI systems. I'd want my loan cleared before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work hard for the startup for two years and take on customer-facing work. Then I'd either launch a product or join a bigger firm that wants an engineer who understands hardware, software and AI. I'd pay 200 a month on the loan, and I'd keep 500 aside before I took any risks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Energised, in the end. Five years feels like a good length for a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why 500 aside before taking risks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm comfortable with risk, but not with an empty account. Five hundred is two weeks of rent and food, and it means I can say no to a bad job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you want on your side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My old professor, Dr Haruko, who runs the racing team. She knows everyone in the hardware industry, and she'd tell me honestly if I was kidding myself.

say: Five years is enough to act, and the next elections should be about **retraining** and fair rules.
I'd say so to anyone who'll listen.
think: I see it as a **window** to gain real experience while the startup is alive.
do: Launch a product or join a firm needing **hardware and AI** skills.
Pay 200 a month on the loan and keep **500 aside**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway, and I'd say so. I'd tell friends to use it, and I'd tell governments to treat the decade as a gift and not a delay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be 32, and I'd expect to have built something, or to be senior in a firm that uses AI well. The risk I see isn't that I'd be left behind, but that the benefits would go only to owners. That's what I'd keep an eye on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay off the loan within six years, then invest a bit. I'd keep learning AI tools as they change and take a part-time degree in robotics or systems engineering, since robots arrive in 2039 and hardware experience then matters. I'd also be active in my union branch and in politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. I'd still be thinking about it, but it wouldn't wake me at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the risk is that benefits go to owners. What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Vote, organise and argue. I'd also put some money into a worker-owned co-op if one existed in my field, because I'd rather own a piece of the thing than watch someone else own all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why robotics, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because by 2039 the robots are the new wave, and someone has to install them, fix them and say what's safe. I already like hardware, so it's an easy step.

I'd tell friends to use the time.
think: The real risk isn't being left behind but the benefits going to **owners** only.
At 32 I'd expect to have built something or be **senior** somewhere.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there'd be no gap to build a cushion and my loan would still be there. What would help is a pause on loan payments if work disappears, and public money for people to retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people my age aren't passive. A lot of us are building things on our own and using the tools daily, and we'd like the older people in charge to treat this like a real emergency.

headlineQuote: A lot of us are building things on our own and using the tools daily
portrait: Nikhil, 22, is a top-of-the-class electrical engineering graduate working at a seven-person **sensor startup** in Bristol.
He has heavy student debt, shares a flat with three people and has about two weeks of savings.
He is progressive and adaptive, using AI tools every day and building side projects.
His main worry is the startup's money, and his plans lean toward products, **hardware** and robots.
He is anxious when time is short and calm only with ten years, while worrying about who owns the gains.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario worries him most, since there would be no time to clear the loan or build a cushion.
whatWouldHelp: A **pause on loan payments** if work disappears, and public money for people to retrain.
